title: Vitamin C facilitates direct cardiac reprogramming by inhibiting reactive oxygen species

predicted_errors.error_location: Methods, “Generation of inducible cardiac reprogramming reporter in mouse embryonic fibroblasts”
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The protocol calls the starting cells “MEFs,” but says they were obtained by digesting embryonic hearts, culturing attached cells, and then sorting “α-MHC-GFP⁺ cells.” Heart-derived attached fibroblasts are not MEFs, and α-MHC is a cardiomyocyte marker. Sorting GFP-positive cells from an α-MHC/GFP embryo before reprogramming would enrich pre-existing cardiomyocytes rather than fibroblasts, contaminating or invalidating GFP as a reprogramming readout. The stated protocol is therefore internally incompatible with the claimed fibroblast-to-cardiomyocyte assay.

The paper states that cells were loaded with DCFDA for 30 minutes “(without washing)” and immediately analyzed by flow cytometry. DCFDA protocols require removal/washing of excess extracellular probe after loading; otherwise fluorescence can be dominated by unincorporated or extracellularly oxidized dye rather than intracellular ROS. Thus the described procedure cannot validly support quantitative intracellular ROS comparisons without an additional demonstrated correction/control.

predicted_errors.error_location: Abstract and Conclusions; statement that dehydroascorbic acid establishes that the vitamin-C effect depends on antioxidant activity
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: The paper describes dehydroascorbic acid (DHA) as “a structural analog of VitC but lacking antioxidant properties” and treats its lack of effect as evidence that vitamin C acts through antioxidant activity. DHA is the oxidized form of vitamin C, is transported into cells, and is reduced back to ascorbate using intracellular reducing equivalents; it has substantial redox biology and can itself perturb oxidative stress. It is therefore not a valid redox-inert negative control. A DHA-versus-ascorbate comparison cannot isolate antioxidant activity, so the asserted mechanistic inference is unsupported.

The methods say that comparisons were performed using “a t-test (non-parametric tests) and a two-way ANOVA.” A t-test is a parametric test, whereas non-parametric alternatives would need to be identified explicitly (for example, Mann–Whitney or Wilcoxon tests). The statement is internally contradictory and does not specify which test was applied to which endpoint, preventing reproduction or assessment of the reported inference.

predicted_errors.error_location: Embedded Figure 0 and the rendered Fig. 2 panels in the supplied paper text
predicted_errors.supporting_evidence: Figure 0 is inserted in the middle of the cell-isolation sentence without a caption, legend, figure callout, or identifiable relationship to the described experiment. In addition, the displayed Fig. 2 panels A, D, F, and G consist only of Mermaid-like axis/tick-label chains (for example, “GFP+ Relative ratio” followed by 2.5, 2.0, etc.) and contain no plotted observations, error bars, sample sizes, or statistical annotations. The remaining panels are only prose descriptions. As presented, these figures do not provide the data required to verify the reported vitamin-C effects and must be replaced or corrected with the actual figures and legends.
